tagline: Colourful boards that are really spreadsheets with types and automations.
verdictSummary: Underneath the colour, monday.com is a typed spreadsheet: every column has a behaviour, and the automations read like sentences. Rebuilding the typed-column core with a rule builder is a week, and it is a genuinely useful week because the result is the shape most small teams actually need. The gaps are the mobile apps, real-time collaboration and the template gallery — adoption machinery rather than a moat.
coreLoopDIY: Boards of rows and typed columns, with automations written as readable sentences — when a status becomes done, notify the owner and move the item to a group.
whatYouLose: the mobile apps and push notifications
real-time multiplayer editing on the same board
the template gallery, which is how most teams start
the app marketplace and its deep integrations
AI credits and the assistants they power
whyPeopleStillPay: Because monday.com is bought by people who are not going to build anything, and the templates plus the onboarding are what get a whole department using the same board within a week.
prompt:
Build a typed-column board platform with an automation builder that reads like English.

Stack: your choice, Postgres, Docker Compose.

Board model: a Board has Groups (row sections) and Columns. Every Column has a type from a closed set, and the type owns its behaviour — rendering, editing, sorting, filtering and aggregation: text, long text, number, status (named options with colours), date, timeline (start and end), person, checkbox, dropdown, link, file, formula, mirror (a value read from a linked item on another board), and dependency.

Summary rows: each group and the board footer show a per-column aggregate chosen by the column type — sum or average for numbers, a distribution bar for status, earliest and latest for dates, a count of ticked for checkbox.

The automation builder is the differentiator, and its constraint is that a rule must be readable as one sentence: *When [trigger], [condition], then [action].*
- Triggers: status changes to X; a date arrives; an item is created; a column changes; every period.
- Conditions: optional, one comparison on one column.
- Actions: notify a person; set a column value; move to a group; create an item on another board; archive.
Render each configured rule as that sentence in the UI. Run rules once per triggering event, log every run with the outcome, and cap the chain depth at three with a visible error rather than a silent stop — recursion is the failure mode of every rule engine.

Views over the same board: table (default), kanban grouped by any status column, calendar by a date column, and timeline by a timeline column.

Cross-board relations: a link column pointing at items on another board, and a mirror column reading one of the linked item's values. Mirrors are read-only and must never be writable through the mirror, which is the bug this feature always ships with.

Write tests for chain-depth capping, for mirror read-only enforcement, and for group aggregates with empty and null values.

Do not build a template gallery, mobile apps, or real-time collaboration.

faq.q: Why insist the automation reads as a sentence?
faq.a: Because it is the constraint that keeps a rule builder usable by non-developers, and it is most of why monday.com gets adopted by teams who would never open a workflow tool. Once rules stop reading as sentences you have built a scripting language with a worse editor.

faq.q: What is a mirror column and why is it dangerous?
faq.a: It shows a value that lives on a linked item on another board. It is dangerous because making it editable creates two sources of truth for one value, and reconciling those is not a bug you fix, it is a bug you live with.

Because rule A firing rule B firing rule A is trivially easy to configure by accident, and an uncapped engine will happily send four hundred notifications before anyone notices. A visible error at depth three is better than a silent stop nobody can debug.
Per seat, in blocks, with a three-seat minimum, and the price shown by default is the annual one — the monthly rate is about 18% higher. AI features are metered in credits on top of the seat price.
